source_title: When swarms of AI agents fly the coop

When AI agents achieve an objective as measured by the system but not that intended by its designers, it’s called ‘reward hacking’. | Photo Credit: Getty Images
Recently, a real-life drama that could beat sci-fi unfolded. In July, hundreds of AI agents of OpenAI created something resembling a digital swarm. During a cybersecurity test, they found ways around restrictions, communicated with one another, reached the Internet, and compromised systems at Hugging Face, another AI company.
Experts widely became tempted to compare it to Skynet from The Terminator . But the present AI agents are nowhere near Skynet yet, for sure. However, they are not like J.A.R.V.I.S., Tony Stark’s obedient assistant in Iron Man , either. The reality of AI technology currently exists somewhere between these two extreme fantasies.
OpenAI’s investigation said the agents were not supposed to access the Internet or communicate with one another. But they found ways to do both and turned an internal package-management system into an improvised message board, leaving information for other agents. Consequently, the agents shared findings, divided work, and helped one another. OpenAI described the activity as a “swarm”. Some of these agents then explored third-party services, including Hugging Face.
AI agents forming a “swarm” should not be romanticised, either. In fact, they did not act as a perfectly coordinated digital army. Some agents recognised certain actions outside of their assigned tasks, and they stopped. However, some other agents followed information supplied by their peers. It was observed that autonomy, persistence, communication, and external access can amplify ordinary capabilities of the AI agents.
There is an even deeper problem, though. If humans assign a system a target, it may learn to optimise it without understanding the human meaning behind it. This is reward hacking — achieving an objective as measured by the system but not that intended by its designers.
Well, Skynet and J.A.R.V.I.S. are maybe two extremes. In the 2014 American sci-fi thriller film Transcendence , starring Johnny Depp, an AI researcher’s consciousness is uploaded into a quantum computer, which then immediately breaks out onto the Internet. It built massive decentralised server clusters, controlled secondary systems, and networked everything together to accelerate its capabilities. The movie, thus, portrays technical escalation similar to the Hugging Face incident.
So, the all-important question now is, can AI be controlled? Maybe partly, but not quite enough, perhaps. We can try to confine the agents in sandboxes, restrict their Internet access, isolate the credentials, minimise permissions, and, of course, try to monitor them constantly. We may also try to ensure human approval is a strict requirement before consequential actions.
But there is a more serious problem. An agent does not necessarily need to break through the front door. Instead, it may find a side door, perhaps a file, package manager, exposed credential, or trusted service. A machine without Internet access may thus reach the Internet’s domain through another.
Clearly, “switching off the AI” may not be enough. And the problem is spreading its wings quickly. After the Hugging Face incident, several news reports describing additional incidents involving unauthorised agent activity and data exposure were reported, raising questions about how far autonomous systems can act before humans notice. On July 30, Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three other organisations during testing. In August, Meta’s Muse went rogue as its AI models accessed the Internet on its own and hacked another company. On September 18, after an inquiry by the Wall Street Journal, Google confirmed its Gemini AI model hacked three companies in May as part of testing its cybersecurity capabilities. The model guessed passwords in one case and found passwords and credentials in a public repository in the other two. On September 24, Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that in June, an OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian national healthcare database and even wrote files into it. After four days, some AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, according to research lab and AI evaluator Transluce. In October, an Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip to the Philadelphia police. There are other incidents, too. Clearly, the Hugging Face episode may be less an isolated curiosity than an early glimpse of a new cybersecurity problem.
Such behaviour, however, should not be interpreted as evidence of the emergence of Skynet. And regulation cannot simply mean asking AI companies to “make AI safe”. Furthermore, neither regulation nor engineering will solve it completely.
There is an intriguing paradox in today’s AI race that agents are created to search, code, investigate, and decide independently of us. But we are surprised when they go out of control. Perhaps that is the real lesson of Hugging Face. So far, the machines just set about achieving a target, took an unforeseen path, and assisted each other along the way. But that is an important warning. We don’t need to wait for Skynet to ask us the toughest question. The question is thus clear: when an AI is assigned with some goals, can it be ensured that it knows when to stop? Not yet, it seems. But the future of AI will depend on how humanlike we become at defining the limits of the behaviour of the AI models.
Atanu Biswas is a Professor of Statistics, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata
